title: Repairing a cracked concrete doorstep with mortar
subtitle: Fill and re-face a cracked or spalled concrete doorstep with a sand and cement repair mortar
excerpt: How to repair a cracked concrete doorstep or threshold slab. Covers cutting back loose concrete, priming with PVA or SBR bonding agent, mixing and applying repair mortar, and finishing with a trowel.
sourceNotes: Cassell's Cyclopaedia of Mechanics (1880s, public domain). UK trade practice for concrete repair.

glossaryTerms.definition: The flaking or breaking away of the surface layer of concrete or masonry, caused by water penetrating the surface, freezing, and expanding. Common on horizontal surfaces such as steps and copings that hold water. Repair requires cutting back all loose material before applying fresh mortar.

Styrene-butadiene rubber emulsion used as a primer and additive for cementitious repair mortars. Applied as a dilute primer coat before the repair to help the new mortar bond to old concrete. Also added to the mixing water to improve adhesion and reduce shrinkage cracking in the repair mortar.

content.text: concrete doorstep is repaired by cutting back all loose concrete, priming the substrate with
, and applying a sand and cement repair mortar in one or two coats. The work takes an afternoon; the step can be used lightly after 24 hours.
Cut back and clean the damage

Tap the cracked area with a hammer: any hollow sound means that section is delaminated and must come off. Use the angle grinder (fitted with a diamond cutting disc) to cut a square or rectangular perimeter around the damaged area to a depth of at least 15 mm. This gives the repair mortar a keyed edge rather than a feathered edge, which prevents the repair lifting at the margins. Remove all loose material with a hammer and cold chisel. Blow out the dust and wash the substrate with clean water.

Brush SBR bonding agent diluted 1:1 with water over the entire repair area, including the cut edges. Allow to become tacky (roughly 20 to 30 minutes) but do not let it dry. The repair mortar should be applied into the tacky primer, not onto a dried film. If the primer dries out before you are ready to apply mortar, apply a second coat.
Mix and apply the repair mortar

Mix 3 parts sharp sand to 1 part cement. Substitute some of the mixing water with undiluted SBR bonding agent (about 20% of the mix water) to improve adhesion and reduce shrinkage. Mix to a stiff but workable consistency. For deep repairs over 25 mm, fill in two layers, allowing the first to stiffen before adding the second. Trowel the mortar firmly into the cut-back area, compact it well, and strike off level with the surrounding concrete. Finish by drawing the flat of the trowel across the surface for a smooth finish.

Cover the repair with a damp cloth or polythene sheet for 24 to 48 hours to slow drying. This reduces shrinkage cracking. Do not allow the repair to dry out quickly in hot or windy conditions. The step can take light foot traffic after 24 hours but should not have heavy use for seven days until the mortar has gained strength.

attrs.symptom: Repair mortar crumbles or fails to bond within a few months
attrs.cause: Feathered edge around the repair area, poor surface preparation, or no bonding agent used.
attrs.fix: Cut back more aggressively to a minimum 15 mm depth with square cut edges. Always use SBR bonding agent as a primer.

attrs.symptom: Surface cracks appear in the repair as it dries
attrs.cause: Mortar mix was too rich in cement (too strong relative to the old concrete) or dried too quickly.
attrs.fix: Fine surface cracks are normal. Wide cracking indicates the mix was too dry or cured too fast. Cover the next repair with polythene and dampen daily for 48 hours.
